source_text: Tamen, sicut supra diximus, doleamus necesse est, quod nulla civitas impune latura sit sanguinis nostri effusionem; sicut et sub Hilariano praeside, cum de areis sepulturarum nostrarum adclamassent: Areae non sint! areae ipsorum non fuerunt! Messes enim suas non egerunt. Ceterum et imbres anni praeteriti quid commemoraverint genus humanum apparuit, cataclysmum scilicet et retro fuisse propter incredulitates et iniquitates hominum, et ignes, qui super moenia Carthaginis proxime pependerunt per noctem, quid minati sint, sciunt qui viderunt, et pristina tonitrua quid sonaverint, sciunt qui obduruerunt. Omnia haec signa sunt imminentis irae dei, quam necesse est, quoquo modo possumus, ut et nuntiemus et praedicemus et deprecemur interim localem esse. Universalem enim et supremam suo tempore sentient qui exempla eius aliter interpretantur. Nam et sol ille in conventu Uticensi extincto paene lumine adeo portentum fuit, ut non potuerit ex ordinario deliquio hoc pati positus in suo hypsomate et domicilio. Habetis astrologos. Possumus aeque et exitus quorundam praesidum tibi proponere, qui in fine vitae suae recordati sunt deliquisse, quod vexassent Christianos. Vigellius Saturninus, qui primus hic gladium in nos egit, lumina amisit. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, cum, indigne ferens uxorem suam ad hanc sectam transisse, Christianos crudeliter tractasset, solusque in praetorio suo vastatus peste convivis vermibus ebullisset, Nemo sciat, aiebat, ne gaudeant Christiani aut sperent Christianae. Postea cognito errore suo, quod tormentis quosdam a proposito sue excidere fecisset, paene Christianus decessit. Caecilius Capella in illo exitu By(??)mtinor, Christiani gaudete (??) exclamavit. Sed qui videntur sibi impune tulisse, venient in diem divini iudicii. Tibi quoque optamus admonitionem solam fuisse, quod cum Adrumeticum Mavilum ad bestias damnasses, et statim hace vexatio subsecuta est et (??)nc en eadem causa interpellatio sanguinis. Sed memento de cetere.
thought_title: Warnings from past judgments and the case of Mavilus
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Scapula, the proconsul of Africa, and has just said Christians await vengeance from God; now he warns that no city will shed Christian blood with impunity and gives examples of divine signs and the fates of persecuting governors.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless, as we said above, it is necessary that we grieve, because no city will bear with impunity the shedding of our blood; just as also under the governor Hilarianus, when they had cried out about the areas of our burial grounds: 'Let there be no areas!' their own areas did not exist! For they did not bring in their harvests. Moreover, what the rains of the past year reminded the human race of has appeared, namely that a flood also happened in the past because of the unbeliefs and iniquities of men, and what the fires, which recently hung over the walls of Carthage through the night, threatened, those who saw them know, and what the former thunderclaps sounded, those who hardened themselves know. All these things are signs of the impending wrath of God, which it is necessary, in whatever way we can, that we both announce and proclaim and pray that it is for the time being local. For the universal and final one those will feel in their own time who interpret its examples otherwise. For also that sun in the assembly at Utica, with its light almost extinguished, was so great a portent that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, being placed in its own exaltation and dwelling. You have astrologers. We can equally also set before you the ends of certain governors, who at the end of their life remembered that they had done wrong, because they had harassed Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, who first here drove the sword against us, lost his eyesight. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, when, taking it badly that his wife had gone over to this faith, he had treated Christians cruelly, and alone in his palace, ravaged by plague with worms, he had boiled over with living worms, he kept saying: 'Let no one know, lest the Christians rejoice or the Christian women hope.' Afterwards, having recognized his error, because he had made some fall away from their purpose by tortures, he died almost a Christian. Caecilius Capella in that end of By(??)mtinor cried out: 'Christians, rejoice!' But those who seem to themselves to have borne it with impunity will come to the day of divine judgment. For you too we hope that the only warning was this, that when you had condemned Mavilus of Hadrumetum to the wild beasts, and immediately this affliction followed and now behold from the same cause the interpellation of blood. But remember for the future.

choices.why: The word means open grounds or plots; here it refers to Christian burial grounds, and the crowd's cry plays on the same word for their own fields, so 'areas' preserves the repetition.
The glossary requires 'faith' for secta, the Christian way of life as viewed by outsiders.
The verb vexo means to harass or mistreat, fitting the governors' persecution of Christians.
The glossary requires 'torture' for tormenta, the means used to force Christians to deny their faith.
The glossary requires 'wild beasts' for bestiae, the arena animals to which condemned Christians were thrown.
The glossary requires 'wrath of God' for ira dei, the divine wrath Tertullian warns will fall on persecutors.

pass_b_english: Yet, as I said above, we cannot help grieving that no city will allow our blood to be shed with impunity. So it was under the governor Hilarianus, when the crowds cried out about our burial grounds: "Let there be no burial grounds!" Their own burial grounds were not there, for they did not bring in their harvests. As for the rains of last year, what they reminded the human race of is plain enough: that a flood came long ago because of human unbelief and iniquity. And the fires that recently hung over the walls of Carthage through the night—those who saw them know what they threatened, and those who hardened themselves know what the ancient thunderclaps sounded. All these are signs of the coming wrath of God, which we must announce, proclaim, and pray may be local for the time being, in whatever way we can. For those who interpret these examples otherwise will feel the universal and final wrath in its own time. Even that sun in the assembly at Utica, when its light was almost extinguished, was such a portent that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, positioned as it was in its exaltation and home. You have your astrologers.

I can likewise set before you the ends of certain governors, who at the close of their lives remembered that they had done wrong in harassing Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, who first used the sword against us here, lost his eyesight. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, indignant that his wife had gone over to this faith, treated Christians cruelly; and when he was left alone in his palace, ravaged by plague with worms boiling out of him, he said, "Let no one know, so that Christians do not rejoice or hope." Later, when he recognized his error—that he had made some fall from their purpose through torture—he died almost a Christian. Caecilius Capella cried out at that departure of his, "Christians, rejoice!" But those who think they have escaped unpunished will come to the day of divine judgment.

We also hope that for you this has been only a warning: that when you condemned Mavilus of Hadrumetum to the wild beasts, this harassment followed at once, and now in the same cause comes a summons for blood. But remember for the future.
notes: The source contains OCR damage: 'By(??)mtinor' and '(??)nc en' are uncertain readings. The gloss renders what is legible and marks the damage.
The phrase 'Caecilius Capella in illo exitu By(??)mtinor' is corrupt; the place name cannot be securely restored.

problems.source_quote: Areae non sint! areae ipsorum non fuerunt!
problems.fix: Let there be no burial grounds! Their own burial grounds were not there!

problems.quote: so that the Christians do not rejoice or the Christian women hope.
problems.source_quote: ne gaudeant Christiani aut sperent Christianae
problems.why: English adds "women" which is not present in the Latin.
problems.fix: so that Christians do not rejoice or hope.
problems.ruling: "Christianae" is feminine plural; "Christian women" is correct, not an addition. The reported problem itself is wrong.

edits.new: Let there be no burial grounds!

edits.old: Their own areas came to nothing
edits.new: Their own burial grounds were not there

edits.old: so that the Christians do not rejoice or the Christian women hope.
edits.new: so that Christians do not rejoice or hope.

fixed: Changed 'Let them have no areas!' to 'Let there be no burial grounds!' because the source 'areae sepulturarum' refers to burial grounds, not generic areas.
Changed 'Their own areas came to nothing' to 'Their own burial grounds were not there' to match 'areae ipsorum non fuerunt'.

Removed 'women' from 'so that the Christians do not rejoice or the Christian women hope' because the Latin 'ne gaudeant Christiani aut sperent Christianae' has no word for women; 'Christianae' is simply the feminine plural of 'Christianus'.

problems.quote: cried out at that departure of the Byzantines
problems.why: Source is corrupt but likely means 'at that death/departure of his'; 'Byzantines' is not supported by context.
problems.fix: cried out at that departure of his
problems.ruling: Corrupt "By(??)mtinor" likely not "Byzantines"; translator adds unsupported group.

problems.quote: no city will shed our blood with impunity
problems.source_quote: nulla civitas impune latura sit sanguinis nostri effusionem
problems.why: English reverses agency; Latin says no city will allow the impune shedding of our blood, not that the city will shed the blood itself.
problems.fix: no city will allow our blood to be shed impunely
problems.ruling: Latin 'latura sit' = 'will bear/tolerate'; English 'will shed' wrongly makes the city the agent of shedding, reversing the meaning.

edits.old: cried out at that departure of the Byzantines
edits.new: cried out at that departure of his

edits.old: no city will shed our blood with impunity
edits.new: no city will allow our blood to be shed with impunity

fixed: Changed 'cried out at that departure of the Byzantines' to 'cried out at that departure of his': source 'in illo exitu By(??)mtinor' is corrupt but contextually refers to Caecilius Capella's own death, not Byzantines.

Changed 'no city will shed our blood with impunity' to 'no city will allow our blood to be shed with impunity': source 'nulla civitas impune latura sit sanguinis nostri effusionem' means no city will bear with impunity the shedding of our blood; the city is not the agent of shedding.

problems.quote: and now the same cause brings a demand for blood.
problems.source_quote: et (??)nc en eadem causa interpellatio sanguinis
problems.why: Source says 'and now in the same cause an interpellation of blood'; 'interpellatio' implies a divine summons or challenge, not merely a 'demand'.
problems.fix: and now in the same cause comes a summons for blood.
problems.ruling: source has “interpellatio sanguinis” (a summons/call of blood), not a simple “demand for blood”

edits.old: and now the same cause brings a demand for blood.
edits.new: and now in the same cause comes a summons for blood.

fixed: The English 'demand for blood' misstates 'interpellatio sanguinis', which is a summons or challenge, not a demand; changed to 'summons for blood'.
